name: Feudal Europe
title: Social Hierarchy of Feudal Europe: From King to Serf
in: a feudal kingdom of western Europe
period: c. 1000–1300 (the High Middle Ages in France, England and the German lands)

tiers.name: The king
tiers.you: You are anointed king and the great lords owe you homage, but you must keep them loyal, do justice and defend your realm, and you spend your life on the road with your court.
tiers.kid: Kings were crowned in church and ruled with the help of great lords, who promised to be loyal to them.
tiers.rise: The crown passed by inheritance in France and England, though William the Conqueror won England by conquest in 1066. In the German lands the princes elected the king, often choosing his predecessor’s son.
tiers.why: Kings were anointed with holy oil at their coronation, which set them apart from every lord, and they were expected to defend the Church, keep the peace and do justice.

tiers.name: Great lords
tiers.you: You hold castles and many manors, judge the people of your lands and lead your own knights, but you owe the king homage, counsel and soldiers, and a rebel can lose everything.
tiers.kid: Great lords such as dukes and counts lived in castles, ruled large lands and led knights for the king.
tiers.rise: Most great lords inherited their lands, in England and Normandy usually whole to the eldest son. Kings raised favoured servants and soldiers into their ranks, often by marriage to an heiress, and could confiscate the lands of rebels.
tiers.why: The great lords were the dukes, counts and barons who held whole provinces or clusters of manors, often directly from the king.
people: Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester

tiers.name: Bishops and abbots
tiers.you: You rule a diocese or a great abbey with wide estates, advise the king and answer only to church courts, and like most prelates you were probably born into a noble family.
tiers.kid: Bishops and abbots led the Church and its monasteries, owned great lands and often advised kings.
tiers.rise: Bishops were elected by the clergy of their cathedrals and abbots by their monks, though kings and great lords often decided the choice. Learning and royal service could carry a man of modest birth to these offices: Thomas Becket, a London merchant’s son, became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1162.
tiers.why: Bishops governed the dioceses of the Church, and abbots and abbesses the great monasteries.

tiers.name: Knights
tiers.you: You hold a manor from your lord, ride to war in mail armour when he calls, usually for forty days a year, and live from the labour of the peasants on your land.
tiers.kid: Knights were warriors who fought on horseback and were given land in return for serving their lord.
tiers.rise: Most knights were sons of knights, though in the 11th century the word could still cover any armed horseman in a lord’s service, and commoners were sometimes knighted for bravery in war. A landless younger son could make his fortune in tournaments and war, as William Marshal did.
tiers.why: Knights were mounted warriors in mail armour, the elite of every army.

tiers.name: Priests, monks and nuns
tiers.you: You serve a village church or live in a monastery under its rule, keeping the daily round of prayer; you may not marry, and if accused of a crime you answer to the Church’s courts.
tiers.kid: Priests looked after village churches, while monks and nuns lived together in monasteries, praying and working.
tiers.rise: The Church was the career most open to talent: a boy of humble birth could become a priest, a monk or a scholar. Since clergy could not marry, the rank was the man’s alone and passed to no heirs.
tiers.why: Below the prelates stood the great body of the clergy: parish priests, cathedral canons, clerks in minor orders, and the monks and nuns of hundreds of religious houses.

tiers.name: Townspeople
tiers.you: You live in a walled, chartered town, work at a trade your guild regulates, and share the townspeople’s freedoms: your own market, courts and council.
tiers.kid: Townspeople were merchants and craftspeople, and many towns won the right to run their own markets and councils.
tiers.rise: Many peasants moved to the towns, and in England a serf who lived for a year and a day in a chartered borough became free. The sons of rich townsmen could rise through the Church or royal service.
tiers.why: Walled towns grew fast from the 11th century, and their people did not fit the three orders.

tiers.name: Jewish communities
tiers.you: You live in a town under the ruler’s protection, perhaps lending money or trading, but he can tax you at will, and after 1215 you must wear dress that marks you out.
tiers.kid: Jewish families lived in many towns, but rulers taxed them heavily and in 1290 forced them to leave England.
tiers.rise: Standing in the community came from learning and wealth, but both rested on the ruler’s protection, which a new tax, a confiscation or an expulsion could end.
tiers.why: Jewish communities lived in the towns of France, England and the Rhineland, outside the Christian orders and under the protection of the ruler.

tiers.name: Free peasants
tiers.you: You hold your land for a money rent, pay your tithe and attend the manor court, but you are free: you may leave, sell your land or marry without paying your lord.
tiers.kid: Free peasants farmed land and paid rent to a lord, but they could move away or marry without asking him.
tiers.rise: Prosperous free families added to their land and sent sons to the towns or the Church; in hard times, debt or a lord’s pressure could push free men into serfdom.
tiers.why: Free peasants held land without the marks of serfdom.

tiers.name: Serfs and villeins
tiers.you: You hold a house and strips in the village fields, but you must work part of each week on your lord’s land, pay a fine when your daughter marries, and may not leave without his leave.
tiers.kid: Serfs were farmers who had to work on their lord’s land and could not move away without his permission.
tiers.rise: A serf could buy his freedom, be freed by his lord or run away: in England one who lived for a year and a day in a chartered town became free. From the late 13th century many lords took money in place of labour services, and serfdom faded in western Europe after the Black Death of 1348.
tiers.why: Most peasants were dependent tenants of a lord, and many were serfs, legally unfree, whose children inherited their status.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You belong to your lord, who can sell you; you work for him full-time, hold no land and live on what he gives you.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and worked without pay; in England slavery had died out by about 1150.
tiers.rise: Freedom came by manumission, which the Church called a pious act; more often, slaves were turned into unfree tenants with land of their own, and their descendants joined the serfs.
tiers.why: At the start of the period slavery still existed.
